newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian firm produces ethanol from cassava chips.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian firm produces ethanol from cassava chips.

text.p: A Nigerian firm has blazed the trail in becoming the first in Africa to produce ethanol from cassava chips, according to its chief executive.

But Tosan Dafeta, managing director of the Nigerian Yeast and Alcohol Manufacturing Company (NIYAMCO), said at a seminar on cassava in the southwestern city of Ibadan last week that his company was only taking after others in Brazil and India.
"We started this new technology in September 1995 after conducting some research. Now we believe this breakthrough has come to stay on the continent," Dafeta told Reuters.
Ethanol is a primary industrial solvent used in cosmetics, pharmaceutical, perfumes and alcoholic products. It is also used in industrial cooling systems, printing, ink and rubber industries.
It is basically produced from molasses derived from sugar.

Cassava, a root tuber similar to yam and grown on the marginal soils of lowland farms in Nigeria's rain forest and the middle belt states, is a staple food in most homes of the country's 100 million people, Africa's biggest concentration.
Agriculture ministry officials said as the world's largest producer, Nigeria produced 31.4 million tonnes of cassava in 1995.

Dafeta said a decline in supply of molasses from Nigerian sugar companies and increasing local demand for ethanol informed his firm's decision to seek alternative materials for production of the solvent.

Other industry executives at the seminar said given mounting debt problems and costly, imported wheats, their companies had found it adequate to use cassava and its derivatives as substitutes in production of goods.
NIYAMCO was formed in 1973 and is 87 percent owned by Nigerians while the rest of the equity is owned by distillers Bols of Holland, Dafeta said.
He said after NIYAMCO was privatised in 1990 its new board of directors redefined its strategies for survival and growth.
"But lack of capital and industrial hardware have made our daily production level of ethanol to stagnate at 12,000 litres, compared to the local demand of 100,000 litres daily," he said.
"Many local firms rely on imports. By next year, however, we hope to raise our daily production level to almost above half the local demand."

Toyin Bankole, NIYAMCO's quality control manager, explained that in producing ethanol from cassava, the dry chips were milled into flour, liquefied into enzymes and later processed into the fermentation and distillation stages.

He said NIYAMCO could raise its current ethanol production level if it got more tonnes of cassava chips, adding: "We can only get 27,000 tonnes, a far cry from what is required because farmers prefer selling cassava to individuals for consumption."
